title: Thinking like Socrates in the Classroom Education Jnaquin, Rod
author: Jnaquin, Rod
summary: Jnaquin returns to the high school classroom after years away and finds that thirty seconds of genuine curiosity at the door -- asking students what they think, noticed, or care about -- does more work than most instructional frameworks. Drawing on the Stanford Encyclopedia entry on Socrates, Agnes Callard's Open Socrates, and a 2025 Callard-Carpenter conversation, he argues that Socratic practice is not a method to be scheduled and scored but a mode of genuine openness to being changed by what another person says. Callard's concept of 'untimely questions' -- questions about what matters most that we cannot ask ourselves because we already hold answers -- frames why thinking requires other people. Jnaquin's practical argument: Socratic practice should be the baseline of professional life in schools, not a protocol deployed on specific days, because the 'Would You Rather' moment that exposes real contradiction works through the audience's presence and genuine friction -- not the format.
points: Genuine Socratic practice requires the teacher to actually be open to being changed by what students say -- not performing openness as a pedagogical technique but being truly inhabitable by the positions of others, which Callard argues is far rarer than it appears.

Callard's 'untimely questions' explains why you cannot ask yourself the most important questions: you already hold an answer absorbed so early you cannot find its origin, and only a person who does not share your answer can genuinely press you on it.

Embarrassment at self-contradiction -- visible to others in the room -- is the productive lever Callard identifies: this discomfort creates the opening for real thinking, and good debate practice works precisely because the inconsistency is real and the audience is present.

The capitalized Socratic Circle protocol risks converting living inquiry into a scheduled procedure: what made Socrates Socratic was precisely what resists packaging, and the format was never the practice -- the openness was.

When bureaucratic text substitutes for professional conversation in schools (strategic plans, dashboards, rubrics), there is a Socratic problem at institutional scale -- documents cannot answer questions, and teachers and students end up feeling measured rather than thought about.
quotes: My students have been generous with feedback this year, and a pattern keeps surfacing: they say they feel thought about in this class. Seen. Asked. Heard. Several students, unprompted, have offered some version of: 'You actually seem curious about what I think.'

What people argued over after Socrates was gone was not a set of texts or a curriculum. It was the experience of being in conversation with him. The practice could not be reduced to a document, and each generation has had to reconstruct it from the traces left by people who knew him.

Callard argues that Socrates was genuinely open -- not performing openness as a pedagogical technique, but actually inhabitable by the positions of the people he spoke with, actually at risk of being changed by what they said. This is, she insists, far rarer and more demanding than we typically acknowledge.

Most of us, when pressed, hold genuinely contradictory beliefs about the things that matter most -- beliefs we paper over by using different words for the same phenomenon depending on whether we approve of it or not. Socrates's insight was that until someone exposes this wavering through sustained conversation, most people do not know they are wavering at all.

Callard frames Socrates's motto not as 'question everything' -- the most important questions are precisely the ones we cannot question on our own -- but as 'persuade and be persuaded.' That is a harder, more honest formulation, and it changes what productive professional conversation has to look like.

I am not a fan of Socratic Circles -- the capitalized, formalized, protocol-ized version of Socratic practice. Turning Socratic practice into a Proper Noun -- a thing scheduled on certain days, with desks in a specific configuration, observed and scored -- risks converting a living practice of genuine inquiry into exactly the kind of text that cannot answer questions back.

What I am arguing for, both in my classroom and in my ongoing work on teacher collaborative discourse, is that Socratic practice needs to be the baseline of professional life in schools -- not a technique deployed in designated contexts.
